name: Fataluku
confidence_why: Heston 2015, the only instrumental study (four speakers, confirmed in Heston 2015 ICPhS and Heston & Locke 2016), finds no stress, tone or lexical pitch accent and shows that Campagnolo 1973's accent classes, reanalysed as lexical tone by Stoel 2008 for the South dialect, are really syllable-weight differences, but van Engelenhoven & Huber 2020 still call East Fataluku a pitch accent language with predictable initial accent while granting that its word patterns match Heston's Central data, so the remaining disagreement is one of analysis rather than of observed fact.

catalog_quote: As for prosody, I find no convincing evidence for stress in Fataluku, although bimoraic feet play an important role in several aspects of the phonology. Prosody at the word level is governed by accentual phrases (APs), prosodic units containing a single word or a few syntactically close words. ... Chapter 5 deals with the question of word-level prosody, concluding that there is no support for stress, lexical tone or lexical pitch accent in Fataluku. Rather, word-level prosody consists of a high intonational tone whose placement depends on both foot structure and the syntactic and semantic cohesion between adjacent words. ... There is no compelling evidence for tone, lexical pitch accent or any type of lexically-specified word-level prosodic system; rather, pitch contours at the word level depend solely on the intonation. ... sweep_summary: Three title hits for Fataluku (fata1247, catalog 'no-word-stress' on Heston 2015). (1) Heston 2015 PhD is the catalog's own deciding source, already. re-read the Conclusion (p.165-166) and sec. 5.6: no stress, tone or pitch accent, word-level pitch is an intonational H on the second mora of an Accentual Phrase; confirms. (2) Heston 2014 PACLIC 28 (new, downloaded open from ACL Anthology Y14-1046, saved) is a sentence-intonation study of declaratives vs polar questions; on word-level peaks it is explicitly non-committal ('I remain ambivalent about the best phonological analysis of these peaks', pp.397-398) and never claims stress; silent on the classification and superseded by the 2015 dissertation. (3) Roettger, Bruggeman & Grice 2015 (downloaded from the ICPhS 2015 site, paper 197) is about Tashlhiyt Berber; Glottolog attaches it to Fataluku by a computerized keyword assignment from 'disguise' — a false hit to drop. Nothing acquired or unacquired in this search of works with stress in the title supersedes Heston 2015; the classification stands. Standing caveat from the 9/16 check (files already in the same directory, see): other dialects are described differently — van Engelenhoven & Huber 2020 call East Fataluku a pitch accent language with predictable initial/trochaic accent, and Stoel 2008 posits lexical H tone for the South (Lorehe) data of Campagnolo 1973; Heston 2015 argues these peak positions are weight-predictable and postlexical. discovery ran through the ACL Anthology, ICPhS and Glottolog sites directly.

new_statements.quote: On the suprasegmental level, there is no convincing evidence for tone, stress or lexical pitch accent. Pitch contours at the word level are specified by the intonation. Each word (or group of closely connected words) takes by default a single rising-falling intonational contour. I term these intonational units "Accentual Phrases" (APs), following Jun & Fletcher (2015). The intonational rise in each AP peaks on (or just after) the second mora. I analyze this peak as a High intonational tone attached to the right edge of the first foot of each AP (Hft), viewing Fataluku as having bimoraic, left-aligned feet.
new_statements.citation: Heston, Tyler M. 2015. The segmental and suprasegmental phonology of Fataluku. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa.

new_statements.reading: No word stress (and no lexical tone or pitch accent) in Central Fataluku; the second-mora pitch peak is a postlexical intonational H on the first bimoraic foot of an Accentual Phrase, present only when the word is AP-initial. Supports the catalog's 'no-word-stress' coding.

sources.note: Central (Lospalos) Fataluku has no word stress, lexical tone or lexical pitch accent; the f0 peak on the second mora of a word is a postlexical intonational H tone on the right edge of the first bimoraic foot of an Accentual Phrase, and disappears when the word is non-initial in an AP (sec. 5.6). Sec. 5.6.1 argues explicitly that a predictable-stress (weight-sensitive iamb) analysis is untenable because the peak-bearing final syllable of disyllables shows reduction and fewer contrasts.

sources.quote: Regardless of the sentence type, it is common to find a pitch peak in the first or second syllable of each word or short phrase, each generally lower than the peak preceding. These pitch peaks occur in approximately the same locations described by Stoel (2008). However, since his analysis of "tone" resembles an intonation system in some ways, I remain ambivalent about the best phonological analysis of these peaks. (pp.397-398) ... Another important topic is the phonological representation of the pitch peaks that occur in the first or second syllable of a prosodic phrase, whether these represent phonological tone, intonation or something else. (p.402)
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 'Suprasegmental Phonology' p.396; sec. 4.1 p.397-398; sec. 5 Discussion / future research p.402
sources.note: Sentence-level intonation study (six speakers from Lospalos, Com and Muapitin): declaratives end in a short final vowel with L%, polar questions in a lengthened final vowel with L+HL%. On word-level prosody it only notes a pitch peak on the first or second syllable of each word/short phrase and explicitly leaves open whether this is tone, intonation or 'something else'; it never mentions stress for Fataluku. It pre-dates and is superseded by Heston 2015, which settles the question as intonation-only.
